cards.title: 1.1.1 Carbohydrates
body: Carbohydrates are organic compounds made up of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
The elements are in the of 1 C: 2 H:1 O.
Carbohydrates are obtained from sugar cane, milk, bread, potatoes, wheat, pasta, cereals, “injera” and rice.
Monosaccharides join together to form complex carbohydrate molecules, such as disaccharides and polysaccharides, through the process of condensation.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Proteins
body: Just as monosaccharides are the building blocks of polysaccharides, amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.
All amino acids contain an amino group (-NH2), which consists of hydrogen and nitrogen.
Proteins are referred to as nitrogenous compounds, because of the presence of nitrogen in their structure.
The bond between two amino acids is called a peptide bond.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Lipids
body: The most common lipids are fats, oils and waxes.
Like carbohydrates, lipids are composed of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Fats and oils are similar except that fats are solid, while oils are liquid at room temperature.
Fats produce more energy than carbohydrates or proteins.

cards.title: 1.1.4 Minerals
body: Minerals (mineral salts) are important inorganic compounds containing elements which are essential for normal body metabolism.
Examples of mineral elements are iron, calcium, potassium, etc.
Animals obtain these elements from the foods they take in.
Place a small amount of bean seed in a metal cup (crucible). b.

cards.title: 1.1.5 Vitamins
body: Vitamins are organic substances that are important for normal growth and development.
Vitamins are required in very small amounts (traces) in the diet, but their role is vital.
Vitamins were named A, B, C, D, E and K, in order of their discovery, but they are also given chemical names.
Vitamins do not supply energy nor do they help in building the body.

cards.title: 1.1.6 Water
body: Water is the most important nutrient of all living cells.
A water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.
Life on the earth is totally dependent on water.
Water is essential to the existence of living organisms anywhere.

cards.title: The tube
body: Mouth (amylase on starch) → oesophagus (peristalsis) → stomach (acid + pepsin on protein) → small intestine (bile from liver/gall bladder; pancreatic amylase, trypsin, lipase; wall enzymes finish the job; villi absorb) → large intestine (water back into blood) → egestion of faeces.

cards.title: Liver and pancreas are side-offices that dump chemicals into the small intestine. They are not “the tube” itself.
Enzymes by address
body: Mouth = starch. Stomach = protein (needs acid). Small intestine = all three (carb, protein, fat) + bile for fat droplets. “Small intestine does the real absorbing — villi.”

cards.title: More detail — nutrients and the tube
body: Carbohydrates: sugars are already small; starch is a chain that amylase chips into maltose, then maltase finishes glucose. Proteins: pepsin (stomach, pH ~2) and trypsin (intestine, alkaline) cut to peptides, peptidases to amino acids. Fats: bile salts from the liver emulsify (big drops → tiny drops, more surface); lipase then cuts to fatty acids and glycerol. Bile is not an enzyme.

Liver: makes bile, stores glycogen, processes incoming blood from the gut (hepatic portal vein). Pancreas: digestive juice + (later) insulin. Appendix is a dead-end off the caecum — know it exists; don’t invent a major job.

Deficiency sketches: no vitamin C → scurvy; no D / Ca → weak bone; no iron → anaemia; no iodine → goitre (ties to Grade 11 thyroid); no protein in children → wasting. Excess sugar/fat → obesity and later diabetes risk.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Ingestion, Digestion and Egestion
body: The term “soluble” means that a substance can dissolve in a liquid.
Ingestion is the act of eating or taking in food through the mouth.
The break down of large food particles into small, usable molecules is called digestion.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Mechanical and Chemical Phases of Digestion
body: Most often, the food an animal consumes is in large pieces.
The mechanical phase is only a physical change, because the chemical composition of the food remains the same.
Teeth help in the physical (mechanical) breakdown of food, by biting, crushing and grinding.

cards.title: 1.2.4 The Pharynx
body: The pharynx (throat) is a muscular tube connecting the mouth to the oesophagus (gullet), and the nasal cavity to the trachea (windpipe).
The pharynx is located at the back of the mouth, and transports food to the oesophagus.
The tongue rolls food into small round masses called boluses (singular: bolus).

units.title: The Circulatory System
units.intro:
Double circulation: heart → lungs → heart (pulmonary) and heart → body → heart (systemic). Right side is deoxygenated; left is oxygenated. Valves stop back-flow.

Path: body veins → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

lessons.title: The Human Heart and Types of Circulation

cards.title: More detail — heart beat and blood
body: Walls: left ventricle is thickest because it pushes systemic pressure. Atria are thinner receiving rooms. AV valves (tricuspid right, bicuspid/mitral left) stop ventricle-to-atrium backflow. Semilunar valves stop artery-to-ventricle backflow. “Lub-dup” is valves closing.

Heartbeat: atria fill, atria squeeze, ventricles squeeze, pause. Coronary arteries feed the heart muscle itself — a clot there is a heart attack. Pulse is an artery expanding with each ventricle beat.

Red cells: no nucleus in mature human RBCs, packed with haemoglobin. White cells: some phagocytose, some make antibodies. Platelets are fragments. Plasma is pale yellow. Anaemia = too little haemoglobin or too few RBCs. Clotting needs platelets + plasma factors + calcium; hemophilia is a factor missing.

cards.title: 2.1.1 The Human Heart
body: The heart functions as a pump and is responsible for the circulation of blood through the blood vessels.
The heart produces the pressure responsible for making blood flow through the blood vessels by contracting forcefully.
The right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs, where carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen.
Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the lungs and oxygen diffuses from the lungs into the blood.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Types of Circulation
body: In general, in animals there are two types of circulations: open and closed circulation.
The open type of circulation is found in insects, in which the blood does not flow through blood vessels.
In an open circulatory system, blood pumped by the heart is emptied into large blood-filled spaces.

units.title: The Lymphatic System
units.intro:
Capillaries leak fluid into tissues (tissue fluid). Most returns to blood capillaries; the rest becomes **lymph** and is collected by lymph vessels that have valves and pass through **nodes** (filters packed with white cells). Lymph returns to blood near the collarbone veins. Also carries fat from villi (lacteals).

Compared with blood: no red cells, no high-pressure pump — muscles and valves squeeze lymph along. Nodes swell when they are fighting infection.

cards.title: More detail — lymph
body: Tissue fluid is plasma minus most large proteins. At the arterial end of a capillary, pressure pushes fluid out; at the venous end some is sucked back. The leftover is lymph. Vessels start blind-ended, have valves, pass nodes (armpit, neck, groin, mesentery). Spleen and thymus are related lymphoid organs (thymus trains T-cells — Grade 11).
If lymph drainage fails, the limb swells (oedema). After a fatty meal the lymph from the gut looks milky because of lacteals.

cards.title: 3.1.1 Lymph
body: Lymph is a colourless fluid containing water, waste materials, cell products (such as hormones and enzymes), digested fat, lymphocytes and phagocytes, which is transported from the blood capillaries by diffusion and filtration.
Rising osmotic pressure of the tissue fluid interferes with osmotic reabsorption of water in the blood capillaries.
The volume and pressure of fluid in the interstitial spaces then tends to increase.
Once tissue fluid enters the lymphatic vessels, it becomes lymph.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Lymphatic Vessels
body: The lymphatic vessels are formed by the lymphatic capillaries, which unite before entering either the thoracic ducts or right lymphatic duct.
The walls of the lymphatic capillaries, like those of the blood capillaries, consist of a single layer of squamous epithelial cells, but are thinner.
The lining of the small intestine contains specialized lymphatic capillaries called lacteals.
The larger lymphatic vessels lead to specialized organs called lymph nodes.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Lymph Nodes
body: Lymph nodes are bean-shaped organs containing large numbers of leukocytes.
Generally, they occur in groups or chains along the paths of the larger lymphatic vessels throughout the body, but are absent in the central nervous system.
Cervical region: nodes in the cervical region occur along the lower border of the mandible, in front of and behind the ears, and deep within the neck along the paths of larger blood vessels.
Axillary region: nodes in the underarm region (armpit) receive lymph from vessels that drain the upper limbs, wall of the thorax, mammary glands (breasts) and upper wall of the abdomen.

body: The circulatory and lymphatic systems are two different systems.
The function of the circulatory system is to transport nutrients, oxygen and other useful substances.
The system is also used to remove waste substances, such as carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes produced by cells.
The function of the lymphatic system is to keep the fluid balance in the interstitial spaces.
The substances that leak from the capillaries are collected and returned to the blood circulation by the lymphatic system.

tips.text: The lymphatic system is a system consisting of different organs and tissue.
The lymph contains solutes that pass from the blood capillaries. These include ions, nutrients, gases and some proteins; and cell products such as hormones, enzymes and waste products.

The lymphatic system performs the following functions: it helps to keep the fluid balance in the interstitial space, absorbs and transport fat into the blood circulation, and helps in defending the body against diseasecausing agents (as part of the immune system).
The lymph nodes are located at intervals along the lymph and are called lymph glands.
Tonsils form a protective ring of lymphatic tissue around the opening between the nasal and oral cavities. They provide protection against infection in the nose and mouth.
The spleen helps to remove iron from the haemoglobin of the old red blood cells and also produces antibodies against harmful organisms.
The thymus gland plays an important role in the development of the immune response in early life. It is a site of lymphocyte formation and antibody production.

units.title: The Immune System
units.intro:
**Antigen** = foreign marker. **Antibody** = protein shaped to stick to that marker. White cells: some eat pathogens (phagocytes), some remember and make antibodies (lymphocytes).

**Active immunity:** your body meets the antigen (infection or vaccine) and makes its own memory. Lasts. **Passive:** you borrow ready antibodies (breast milk, injection). Fast but short.

cards.title: 4.1 Antigens and Antibodies
body: Anything that can trigger an immune response in the body is called an antigen.
An antigen can be a whole microbe (bacteria or a small parasite, such as a virus) or even a part of a microbe.
Tissue or cells from a donor (apart from an identical twin) can also act as antigens if given to a recipient.
In the recipient’s body, this tissue is capable of triggering an immune response, because it is foreign to the recipient.
Antibodies are protein substances produced by white blood cells in response to antigens.

body: Natural acquired active immunity: This type of immunity is produced when a disease-causing agent is introduced into the body by natural means (non-intentional).

The introduction of serum that contains ready-made antibodies is important for individuals who cannot fight a disease and produce their own antibodies.
In most cases, this type of immunity lasts from a few weeks to several months.

tips.text: Immunity is the ability of the body to resist infection from exposure to a micro-organism or parasite.

Before any foreign particle establishes itself inside the body of an animal, it has to bypass the physical components of the immune system, such as the skin and mucus, and resist chemical defences (tears, mucus secretions and saliva).
Once the foreign particle gets through the physical barriers, the advanced components of the immune system become active and generate specific antibodies.
Antibodies are proteins produced by white blood cells to specifically fight foreign substances known as antigens.
Antigens are macromolecules that induce certain responses in the immune system.

Immunity is the ability of the body to resist an infectious disease. These can be broadly classified as specific or non-specific components. This type of immunity is called innate (inborn or natural) immunity.

The other components of the immune system, adapt themselves to each new disease encountered and are able to generate a specific type of immunity for a specific pathogen or antigen during the lifetime of an individual.
The components of the immune system are grouped in a type of immunity called acquired immunity.

Inborn immunity refers to a phenomenon in which genetic characteristics common to a particular kind of organism or species provide defences against certain pathogens. Such individuals or species are said to have natural immunity.
For example the immunity of the body against many animal diseases (such as hog cholera, cattle plague, and distemper) and the natural immunity of some individuals to tuberculosis.

units.intro:
Nose (warm, filter, moisten) → pharynx → trachea (rings of cartilage) → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli (huge surface, thin, moist, capillary wrap).

**Inhale:** diaphragm down, ribs up and out → chest volume up → pressure down → air in. **Exhale:** opposite (often passive at rest).

cards.title: 5.1.1 The Nose
body: The human respiratory system starts with the nose.
The nose encloses the nasal cavity, which opens to the outside through openings called the nostrils.
The air that enters the body through the nose is warmed, filtered and moistened as it passes through the nasal cavity.
Fine hairs (cilia) lining the cavity filter the inhaled air before it passes down the pharynx.

cards.title: 5.1.2 The Pharynx
body: The pharynx is a tube-like structure, and is a part of both the respiratory and digestive systems.
Air is breathed in through the trachea into the lungs, whereas food passes down the oesophagus to the stomach.
The pharynx extends into a slit or narrow opening, known as glottis, which leads into the larynx.
The opening is guarded by a flap of tissue called the epiglottis.

cards.title: 5.1.3 The Trachea
body: The trachea extends from the neck to the thorax, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi (singular: bronchus).
The two main bronchi enter the right and left lungs.
Inside the lung, each bronchus branches into several bronchioles.
A single layer of epithelial cells lines each alveolus.

cards.title: 5.1.4 The Lungs
body: The branching network of bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli comprise the lungs.
Lungs are respiratory organs found in the thoracic cavity.
The left lung is slightly smaller (because of the heart that is located slightly to the left of the body) and has two lobes.
The right lung is bigger, with three lobes.

units.title: The Excretory System
units.intro:
Excretion removes *metabolic* waste (CO₂, urea, excess salts and water). Egestion is undigested food — different word.

Organs: lungs (CO₂), skin (sweat: salts, a little urea), liver (makes urea from amino acids — deamination), kidneys (filter blood, keep what you still need).

cards.title: 6.1 The Excretory Products
body: All cells carry out metabolic reactions.
If these substances accumulate in the fluid surrounding the cells, they would become toxic (poisonous) and upset the homeostasis of the organism.
Single-celled organisms can remove their waste products by simple diffusion, but large animals require a more elaborate excretory system.
The external environment of a living organism is constantly changing.
The internal environment of the cells (the amount of water, the concentration of glucose, the temperature, etc.) is kept almost constant all the time.

cards.title: 6.2 The Excretory Organs
body: The excretory organs in mammals are the skin, lungs, kidneys and liver.
The skin is considered to be the largest organ because it covers the entire surface of the body.
Human skin is composed of two layers: the epidermis and dermis.
The dermis is an inner layer, which is thicker than the epidermis.

cards.title: The Excretory Organs
body: Kidney: cortex → medulla → pelvis. Nephron: glomerulus filters, tubule reabsorbs glucose/amino acids/most water and salts, collecting duct adjusts water (ADH appears in Grade 11 homeostasis). Urine: water, urea, excess salts — not glucose in a healthy person.

cards.title: Filter then reclaim
body: If glucose appears in urine, the reclaim step failed (or was overloaded) — classic diabetes clue, tied later to insulin.

cards.title: More detail — kidney numbers in words
body: Urea comes from surplus amino acids: liver strips the nitrogen (deamination) and makes urea, which is less toxic than ammonia. Kidneys take a fraction of plasma in the glomerulus (filter under pressure). Useful solutes are pumped back in the tubule. Water follows by osmosis; ADH later fine-tunes the last duct. Bladder stores; sphincter is learned control.
Dialysis mimics the filter when both kidneys fail. Sweat cools you (Grade 11 temperature) and happens to carry some urea — it is not the main urea door.

The medulla is a red colour and divides into a number of funnelshaped, hollow structures, called pyramids.
The dermis is an inner layer, which is thicker than the epidermis.

Excretion is the process of getting rid of the waste products of metabolism.

tips.text: All cells constantly carry out metabolic reactions. These metabolic reactions produce waste products.
The main metabolic wastes in most mammals are carbon dioxide, excess water and salt, urea and red pigments.
Carbon dioxide and excess water are produced during cellular respiration.
The amino acids not used as a source of energy are catabolized in the liver by a process called deamination.
The nitrogen-containing part of the excess amino acid is combined with carbon dioxide and converted into urea, ammonia and uric acid.
The urea dissolves in the blood plasma and is taken to the kidneys to be excreted.
The liver also has many other functions.
The excretory system is responsible for the maintenance of homeostasis by selectively adjusting the concentration of substances in blood and other body fluids.

If allowed to accumulate, metabolic wastes would eventually reach toxic concentrations and upset the homeostasis of the organism. These waste products must, therefore, be removed from the body regularly by the process of excretion.

The excretory organs in mammals are the skin, lungs, kidneys and liver. However, the kidneys are the main excretory organs because they excrete nitrogenous wastes, excess water and mineral salts, and other substances in the form of urine.

units.title: The Sense Organs
units.intro:
Receptors turn a stimulus into a nerve impulse. Skin: touch, pressure, pain, temperature. Nose: chemoreceptors in the air stream. Tongue: taste buds (sweet, salt, sour, bitter — umami may be named). Eye: cornea + lens focus on the retina; rods = dim/black-white; cones = colour in bright light; iris controls pupil. Ear: pinna → canal → drum → ossicles → cochlea (hearing) and semicircular canals (balance).

Internal receptors watch stretch, blood chemistry, posture — they feed homeostasis in Grade 11.

cards.title: More detail — eye and ear
body: Eye path: cornea does most of the bending, lens does the fine focus (accommodation: fat lens for near, thin for far). Iris circular and radial muscles set pupil size. Blind spot = optic nerve exit, no receptors. Short sight: long eyeball, image in front of retina, diverging lens. Long sight: short eyeball or stiff lens, converging lens.

Ear path: air waves → drum → three bones amplify → oval window → fluid in cochlea → hair cells → auditory nerve. Semicircular canals detect rotation (fluid lag). Eustachian tube equalises pressure with the throat.

cards.title: 7.1.1 The Skin
body: The skin is the sense organ which covers the whole body.
For example the fingertips, lips and cheeks have the greatest concentration of receptors and are, therefore, more sensitive to their respective stimuli.
Skin receptors receive a signal and transmit it via nerve cells to the brain.
In the brain, the signals are interpreted as sensations.

cards.title: 7.1.2 The Nose
body: The nasal cavity is lined with mucous membranes that have smell receptors, which are connected to the olfactory nerve.
The smell itself consists of vapours of various substances.
The smell receptors are sensitive to different types of sensations and interact with the molecules of various vapours, transmitting the sensations to the brain through the olfactory bulb.
The chemical molecules of any odorous substance that enter the nose dissolve in the mucus and stimulate the olfactory receptors.

cards.title: 7.1.3 The Tongue
body: The tongue is a sense organ that helps identify taste.
The human tongue is dotted with thousands of taste buds, which are made up of many receptor cells.
Many of the taste buds are found in large swellings, called papillae.
Generally, the taste buds close to the tip of the tongue are sensitive to sweet tastes, whereas those at the back respond to bitter tastes.

cards.title: 7.1.4 The Eye
body: Human eyes are situated in the eye sockets of the skull.
The sockets give protection to the eyes.
A number of muscles hold the eyes in place, enabling them to move in different directions.
The front of the eyeball is covered by a thin, transparent membrane, the conjunctiva.

cards.title: 7.1.5 The Ear
body: The ear is the sense organ that assists in hearing.
The external ear: The external ear consists of the pinna, auditory canal and eardrum (tympanum).
The pinna helps to direct sound waves into the auditory canal.
Glands in the walls of the auditory canal produce a waxy material.

units.title: The Nervous System
units.intro:
Neuron: dendrites collect, cell body integrates, axon carries the impulse, myelin speeds it in many fibres, synaptic knobs dump transmitter onto the next cell. Types: sensory (in), relay (middle), motor (out to muscle/gland).

**CNS** = brain + spinal cord. **PNS** = nerves to the rest. Reflex arc: receptor → sensory → relay (often in spinal cord) → motor → effector. Fast and does not wait for the brain to debate — you still become aware a moment later.

cards.title: 8.1.1 Structure and Characteristics of a Neurons
body: The nervous system is composed of billions of cells, the most basic structure being the nerve cell or neuron.
Neurons or nerve cells that underlie all the activities of the nervous system form a communication network that co-ordinates all the systems of the body.
A typical neuron has all the parts that any cell would have, and a few specialized structures that make it different.
The main portion of the nerve cell is called the soma or cell body.

cards.title: 8.1.2 Types of Neurons
body: Neurons that conduct messages from the sense organs to the brain or spinal cord are called sensory (afferent) neurons.
Different sensory neurons are sensitive to variety of stimuli.
The dendrites of a sensory neuron are usually part of a receptor.
Neurons that conduct messages from the brain or spinal cord to the muscles and glands are called motor (efferent) neurons.

cards.title: 8.1.3 Nerve Impulses
body: Nerves send impulses in response to stimuli.
Every neuron needs a certain minimum amount of stimulus in order to begin transmitting an impulse.
If the stimulus is greater than the threshold, the neuron will respond by sending an impulse.
If the stimulus continues, the neuron will continue to send impulses, one after the other.

cards.title: 8.2.1 The Central Nervous System
body: Brain size is related to body size; larger brains are associated with larger bodies and not with greater intelligence.
The brain,part of the CNS, is housed within the cranium or skull cavity.
In vertebrate embryos, the brain begins developing very early.
The bony skull and three membranes, called the meninges, enclose the brain and protect it.

cards.title: 8.2.2 The Peripheral Nervous System
body: Even though the central nervous system (CNS) receives sensory information, evaluates the information and initiates action, without the peripheral nervous system (PNS), the CNS would remain isolated from both the body and the rest of the world.
The PNS collects information from numerous sources, both inside and outside the body, and relays it by way of afferent nerves to the CNS.
Without the PNS, the CNS would receive no sensory information and could produce no responses.
Even thoughts and emotions could not be expressed because of the CNS’s isolation from various parts of the body.

cards.title: 8.3.1 Inborn Behaviour
body: Inborn behaviour (innate behaviour) does not seem to be influenced by the wide range of environmental differences that exists among individuals.
Taxes (singular: taxis, meaning “movement”) Taxis is a locomotory response of motile cells, like a gamete or whole organism, in response to an external stimulus.
Taxis can be a positive or negative response.
For example the movement of a paramecium toward an acidic region is a positive taxis (positive chemotaxis) and the movement of a cockroach away from light is a negative taxis (negative phototaxis).

cards.title: 8.3.2 Learned Behaviour
body: Learning is an experience-based modification of behaviour.
Learning is characterized by flexibility: what is learned may vary from one individual to another, and the resulting behaviour may be modified if the environment changes.
Certainly, a learned behaviour pattern cannot be inherited, though the ability to learn is almost certainly inherited.
Individuals may improve learned behaviour over time.
